title: IFLA Europe Regional Division Webinar 2026: How EURDC supports Libraries across Europe
raw_text: The IFLA Europe Regional Division invites library professionals, information specialists, and IFLA members from across Europe to an engaging online webinar on 1 October 2026 at 11:00 CEST . Over the past five years, the Europe Regional Division Committee (EURDC) has worked to strengthen collaboration, advocacy, and engagement among libraries and library professionals throughout Europe. Despite these efforts, many colleagues remain unfamiliar with the division’s mandate, activities, and opportunities for involvement. This webinar aims to change that. During the session, four members of the current EURDC Committee, representing Finland, Germany, Norway, and Portugal, will introduce the division’s work and share practical examples of how EURDC supports the European library community. Participants will gain insights into the division’s objectives, ongoing initiatives, and future priorities. The webinar will also provide an opportunity for dialogue. Attendees will be encouraged to share their expectations, discuss challenges facing libraries in Europe, and suggest ways in which EURDC can better support their work and professional communities. The event will be conducted in English via Zoom, with automated subtitles available to improve accessibility. title: The Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) WLIC 2026 Outcomes Report
raw_text: Part of MLAS Members and Attendees at MLAS Business Meeting in Busan The IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) had an active and substantive presence at the IFLA World Library and Information Congress (WLIC) 2026 in Busan. Activities included the MLAS Business Meeting, MLAS Open Session, IFLA Associations Meeting, an informal meeting of International Relations Chairs, and opportunities for congress attendees to connect with the MLAS Chair at the IFLA exhibition booth. Across these activities, common priorities emerged: strategic renewal, member engagement, leadership, partnerships, advocacy, financial sustainability, visibility, digital transformation and AI, resilience, crisis preparedness, and responsiveness to changing societal needs. These priorities are closely aligned with MLAS’s mission to support strong, well-managed library associations through leadership, peer learning, resource development, and effective association practices worldwide. Strong library associations do not simply have strategies. They make their strategies visible, translate them into action, engage their members, build partnerships, advocate effectively, develop new leaders, sustain their organisations, and continually renew themselves in response to change. title: Accountability, Integrity: AI Policy in Public Libraries (New Journal Article)
raw_text: The article linked below was published by Public Library Quarterly. Title Accountability, Integrity: AI Policy in Public Libraries Authors Kathryn FitzGerald University of Washington Benjamin Lee University of Washington Source Public Library Quarterly DOI: 1 0.1080/01616846.2026.2725502 Abstract As artificial intelligence reshapes both library work and the information environment, public libraries must determine whether or how to engage with AI while maintaining library values. To our knowledge, there exists no published analysis of how American and Canadian public library AI policies might link library values and technology adoption. To address this gap, we conducted an environmental scan of public library websites to identify and analyze AI policy statements. Our scan of over 200 library websites identified 32 AI polcies. All reference at least two values, with privacy, security, and responsibility the most frequently cited. title: Report: The Federal Program Keeping Libraries Online? the FCC Might Gut It
raw_text: From the Indianapolis Star: Under the atrium at the Indianapolis Public Library , a woman is busily typing away on her laptop. Another patron seated at the Central Branch is charging their device while streaming music through earbuds as they read quietly between the stacks. Free Wi-Fi allows Hoosiers a cozy and safe place to access the internet at all 26 library locations across Indianapolis. Potential cuts, however, by the Federal Communications Commission have put that access at risk, advocates warn, and not just in Indiana, but for millions of people in libraries and public schools across the country. The FCC recently put into question whether a 30-year-old program that helps keep libraries online should be changed, left alone, or end. No decisions have been reached, but librarians are concerned about what it could mean for their funding. In late June, the FCC issued what appeared to be a benign notice addressing child safety under one of its service operations. Buried within the 86-page document were eight words that sent shockwaves among librarians and educators alike: “Should the E-Rate program be limited or sunset?” [Clip] “This definitely caught us by surprise,” said Jamar Rahming , president-elect of the Public Library Association and CEO of Cuyahoga County Public Library in Cleveland, Ohio. “E-Rate has been just such a fixture in our public library institutions and communities.” Learn More, Read the Complete Article (about 2300 words) The post Report: The Federal Pr

title: Report: “DC Librarian Offers Paid Internship to Boost Interest in Library Science”
raw_text: From WTOP: In 2019, Christopher Stewart started paying students in D.C. to work in a school library and learn about the field. The concept is similar to a paid internship, with students helping with research and shelving books. The goal is to increase students’ awareness of library science and spark their interest in the field. Stewart has brought the program with him to various schools. Now in his first year as senior school librarian at Garnet-Patterson S.T.A.Y. High School, Stewart has opened applications for hiring two library brand ambassadors. He’s already received information from six applicants. The mission, he said, is to “make sure that students have an opportunity to explore the field, particularly Black and Brown students, because we make up so little as far as the grand total of librarians, especially school librarians.” Learn More, Read the Complete Article The post Report: “DC Librarian Offers Paid Internship to Boost Interest in Library Science” appeared first on Library Journal infoDOCKET .

Thank you for all you do in support of libraries, our profession and IFLA. Boy developed "toasted skin" condition from using a laptop every day
raw_text: Fears that modern electronic devices may harm children are nothing new. Gadgets with screens of any size have long been allegedly melting, rotting, and/or corrupting the brains of youths for decades. However, a medical case report published this week offers a new and alarming way our digital doodads may cause physical harm. In BMJ Case Reports , two UK doctors, Mara Znagoveanu and Edward Artley, report the case of a boy who came to an emergency department with alarming marks on his abdomen. The marks were described as being in a patch about 15 centimeters (six inches) wide, made of flat, reddish-brown "interlacing lines forming irregular circles and a lace-like morphology." A picture of the marks is here . Mysterious marks The boy, whom they described only as being in "mid-childhood," was not in any pain, and the rash was not warm to the touch or tender. He and his parents said they couldn't think of any recent injuries or trauma that might explain the marks. He was otherwise healthy, hadn't recently been ill, and had no systemic symptoms, such as fever or fatigue. Everything about the boy's health, growth, and medical history looked normal. title: LinkedIn beats "BrowserGate" lawsuits over scanning users' Chrome extensions
raw_text: LinkedIn beat two lawsuits over its practice of scanning users’ browser extensions, with a judge granting the Microsoft subsidiary's motion to dismiss the cases. The users who sued LinkedIn failed to adequately allege that they have standing to sue because neither asserted that they "had browser extensions installed that conveyed private information to LinkedIn," ruled Judge Vince Chhabria in US District Court for the Northern District of California. In his ruling on Tuesday, Chhabria gave the plaintiffs leave to amend their complaints but said he doubts they can make a plausible case. "Given LinkedIn’s further arguments that users voluntarily download browser extensions, which by their nature intentionally expose data to websites, it seems unlikely that the plaintiffs will ever be able to allege a privacy violation, much less prevail at the end of the day," Chhabria wrote. California residents Nicholas Farrell and Jeff Ganan separately filed class actions against LinkedIn in April, seeking to represent themselves and other LinkedIn users. Ganan's attorney, J.R. Howell, said he is evaluating whether to bring the claims in a California state court, which has different requirements on standing, or to appeal the US district court ruling in the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. title: Bringing Big Ideas Home: Reflections from PLA 2026 in Minneapolis
raw_text: The most valuable takeaway from my time at the Public Library Association Conference wasn’t just new ideas; it was a renewed sense of purpose. As the director of a small, rural library in Elba, Alabama, I was thrilled to receive a PLA scholarship to attend the conference in Minneapolis. PLA has supported our library in meaningful ways over the years, including a 2019 grant that funded a high school intern. That student is now about to graduate from college and, inspired by her experience at our library, is pursuing her MLS. Moments like that are a powerful reminder of the long-term impact of library work. Energy, Inspiration, and Hard Conversations I attended with a colleague from a neighboring library, and from the moment we walked into the Minneapolis Convention Center, the energy was contagious. We immediately felt welcomed, not just by the upbeat registration staff but by the shared sense of purpose among attendees. The opening session set the tone. Hearing from speakers, including Bryan Stevenson, was both inspiring and challenging. His remarks encouraged me to reflect more deeply on local history in my own community, including the possibility of researching and acknowledging difficult chapters like lynchings. I left with a desire to partner with our local historical preservation group to explore ways to honor and remember those stories. title: Europe will go it alone on Venus mission after NASA yanks radar instrument
raw_text: The European Space Agency is moving "full steam ahead" with development of a robotic mission to Venus after NASA officials determined they were unlikely to fulfill a commitment to provide a US-built radar instrument for the spacecraft, the mission's project scientist said. The European orbiter, named Envision, will map the Venusian surface at 10 times higher resolution than the last radar mission sent to Venus by NASA in the 1990s. The planet is enshrouded in a blanket of thick clouds of sulfuric acid, rendering its mysterious surface unseen by optical cameras in orbit. Radar is the most effective way to penetrate the clouds of Venus to reveal the terrain below, and scientists will use Envision to look for signs of active volcanism. NASA and ESA signed a memorandum of understanding in 2024 outlining their partnership on Envision. NASA agreed to supply a US-made synthetic aperture radar instrument, Envision's primary means of mapping the surface of Venus, along with providing tracking and communications support through NASA's Deep Space Network. In exchange, ESA would include US researchers on Envision's science team. Europe would build the Envision spacecraft and the rest of its science instruments and provide the launch on an Ariane 6 rocket. Read full article Comments

raw_text: My name is Lana Sweeting, and I was lucky enough to be selected for a 2026 PLA scholarship. I serve as an Adult Reference Librarian in Portland, Oregon, where much of my work focuses on serving the Black community through programming, collections, and outreach. First, I felt very drawn to the session “Every Story Matters, Every Body Belongs: Fat Inclusive Libraries.” The presenter, Amelia Mason, was absolutely wonderful and very knowledgeable on the subject. I was locked in from the very first slide, which simply said, “I Am Fat.” The honest and positive energy went up from there. Along with sharing quantitative data, Amelia discussed myths surrounding fatness, as well as history, race, fat acceptance and neutrality, and how these issues apply to library spaces and other spaces we regularly occupy. For example, Amelia noted that PLA shirts on the website only went up to size 3XL. After the session, I felt informed and inspired to take this information back to Multnomah County Library. The session included a resource booklist that inspired me to create a booklist and display for my own library and begin conversations around diversity audits of our catalog so we can make relevant materials more accessible. title: Android can now securely migrate your logins between password managers
raw_text: As longer, more complex passwords have become a necessity, remembering all those strings of numbers, letters, and special characters has become nearly impossible. Password managers can solve that problem, but what happens when you want to move to a different login organizer? Sure, you could manually type all your logins into a new app, but now Android can do that for you without the tedium. Google designed the new login transfer process to happen entirely on your phone, so you need the corresponding apps installed with your credentials synced. To start the move, you'll have to find the import option in the app you want to use. The location of that feature will vary, but in Google Password Manager (built into Android), it's near the top under the settings tab. The import option in Google Password Manager will plug in to the new migration system, while export still just creates an unencrypted CSV with your passwords that can be dumped into any app. It will be similar in other apps, so make sure to start the process in the app you want to use. Currently, this works in Google's app, 1Password, Bitwarden, and Dashlane. Read full article Comments

title: Panic builds over bankrupt Spirit’s looming data sale to Google
raw_text: Doug Kreuzkamp was shocked when news outlets reported that Google won an auction to buy a huge amount of operational data as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy proceedings. Kreuzkamp founded a startup called Springshot in 2011, which created a widely used proprietary platform that helps humans and AI systems improve airline efficiency and quickly solve logistics problems so flights can stay on time and airlines can operate as smoothly as possible. Hundreds of airports use it globally. Springshot powered Spirit’s technology stack for the last three years, right up to the “very last flight,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. Yet his company got no notice when Spirit prepared to auction off a massive dataset that he thinks likely improperly includes a substantial amount of data and intellectual property (IP) that Springshot owns—not Spirit. title: Physicist does the math on Star Trek’s “Picard maneuver”
raw_text: It turns out Jean-Luc Picard was an even better starship helmsman than the writers knew. A physicist has gone through the details of a warp-speed trick from the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation and found a subtlety the show missed. But instead of a plot hole, the detail he found actually makes the maneuver more impressive… as well as a great opportunity to teach about a lesser-known feature of the theory of relativity. Níckolas de Aguiar Alves, a physicist at the Federal University of ABC in Brazil, first watched Next Generation as a master’s student. When he got to the episode "The Battle" in the show’s first season, the plot reminded him of his relativity coursework. In "The Battle," a Ferengi leader reminds Picard of a battle he fought years ago as captain of a ship called the Stargazer . Under fire from a mysterious attacker, Picard’s ship’s shields were down. He had to get closer without taking a hit, so he made a gamble. Picard ordered the Stargazer to charge the enemy ship at warp speed (meaning faster than light), then stop abruptly and fire. By going faster than light, Picard anticipated that the other ship would see two images of the Stargazer : where it reached warp speed and where it stopped. If they fired on the wrong image, they would miss the Stargazer , and Picard could win the battle. Read full article Comments

title: Kimmel's ABC show won't air interview with Democrat because of Trump FCC threats
raw_text: ABC's Jimmy Kimmel said he will be interviewing a Democratic candidate for Senate tonight, but the interview will be on YouTube only and not broadcast on TV because of threats made by the Federal Communications Commission. Kimmel has been a prime target in the Trump FCC's attacks on ABC and its owner, Disney. In his monologue last night, Kimmel said he'll be interviewing Democrat James Talarico, a state representative who is running against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton for a seat in the US Senate. In previous years, such an interview would have aired on the broadcast show via local stations throughout the country, Kimmel said. This time, it will only be on the Jimmy Kimmel Live YouTube channel in order to prevent further trouble for individual stations that hold FCC licenses, he said. Read full article Comments

title: AI Is Breaking This Thing We Call Trust
Europese cyberwaakhond kan Mythos 5 na maanden vertraging testen
raw_text: Het Europese cyberbeveiligingsagentschap ENISA krijgt na drie maanden vertraging toegang tot Mythos 5 van Anthropic. Dat AI-model is goed in het opsporen van kwetsbaarheden in ict-systemen. Eerder hadden zowel Anthropic als de Amerikaanse overheid de toegang tot Mythos beperkt.
